newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Tesco snaps up biggest Irish grocer.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tesco snaps up biggest Irish grocer.

text.p: Britain's leading supermarket group Tesco Plc snapped up Ireland's biggest grocery chain on Friday from Associated British Foods (ABF) for 630 million pounds ($1 billion), pleasing the market with promises of higher earnings and better margins.
"It's good news, we are very happy. The shares are still up, which shows the market appreciates the deal," said one analyst who asked not to be named.
However, Tesco shares later closed down one penny at 338 after hitting a high of 346 pence before the announcement, while ABF shares jumped 13-1/2 pence to 525 pence.
The deal is the largest ever in the Irish grocery trade and gives Tesco a 26 percent share of the market in the Irish Republic and 30 percent in Northern Ireland.

Tesco will take control of 75 Quinnsworth and Crazy Prices stores in the Republic as well as 34 stores in Northern Ireland trading as Stewarts, Crazy Prices, Superdeal, Westside Stores and Bloomfield, plus a processing business, an off-licence chain and a sports shop group.
Tesco said it hoped to raise margins in the Irish supermarkets to around six percent in three or four years time from 4.7 percent currently and expected the deal to be earnings enhancing from 1998.

It will add turnover of over one billion pounds to Tesco's current sales of around 12 billion pounds. There are no current plans for job cuts at the Irish stores and Tesco will invest 100 million pounds over the next three years.
Excluding restructuring and integration costs, the acquisition should cover financing costs in the first year, Tesco said in a statement.

ABF finance director Martin Clarke told Reuters that the sale would enable it to focus on its three core businesses, food production, agricultural products and value added food ingredients. The company will receive a 10 million pound dividend before completion of the sale.
"There will be a small dilution to ABF's earnings but they've got a good offer," said Michael Bourke of Panmure Gordon.
Tesco chairman Ian MacLaurin said there had been no decision yet on whether to rename stores under the Tesco brand.
"This is a strong and successful business with a proven management and we look forward to add to that with our own strengths and to continue the success achieved so far," Tesco said in a statement.
Analysts said that Tesco should be able to boost sales per square foot at the Irish shops, with one suggesting it could double Quinnsworth's current 350 pounds per square foot annual turnover.
"Tesco has better buying power and they are better retailers," the analyst said.

ABF chairman Gary Weston said in a statement that there had been several approaches for the business. Private Irish supermarket group Superquinn, which had said it could be interested in bidding, admitted the sale closed the door.
Analysts had been concerned that competition for the grocery stores might push the price up and that Tesco might find it had overpaid.

Tesco, which pushed arch-rival J. Sainsbury Plc out of the market leader slot over a year ago, has earned a reputation for leading the sector with innovations such as loyalty cards and financial services.
Tesco has already opened a city centre "Metro" store in Belfast while Sainsbury has plans for seven outlets in Northern Ireland.
But some analysts said Tesco's foray into Ireland might not be plain sailing with competition evident from both Irish and British groups.

Britain's third largest supermarket chain Safeway has long been rumoured to be interested in buying Wellworth, which operates a chain of stores in Northern Ireland, with a 21 percent share of the market there. ($ = 0.627 British Pounds)
